findings.reason: The protected Python solution determines the maximum font size from a sorted array fonts that allows a sentence text to fit within screen dimensions w and h. It uses Counter(text) to compress repeated character metric queries to at most sigma unique characters, and binary searches over fonts taking advantage of monotone font growth. The solution runs in O(n + sigma * log f) time and O(sigma) space; no candidate is required.

Monotonicity of font height and width ensures binary search on fonts correctly identifies the maximum fitting font size. Character frequency aggregation evaluates total sentence width in at most sigma width queries per candidate font.

Building character frequencies takes O(n) time. Binary search tests O(log f) font sizes with O(sigma) queries per test, yielding O(n + sigma * log f) total time. Auxiliary space is O(sigma) for the frequency map. Complexity evidence is inherited and hash-bound.
Accepts text, w, h, fonts, and fontInfo interface, returning the maximum integer font size that fits or -1 if no font fits.

The approach accurately details character frequency metric compression, binary search over monotone font fit predicates, and O(n + sigma * log f) time / O(sigma) space bounds. Alternatives and edge cases cover linear font scanning overhead, uncompressed per-character query costs, reverse font scanning worst-case risks, boundary dimension equality, height-first rejection efficiency, font value vs index return requirements, and all-font failure handling.

App Python and native Python solutions both execute the identical character frequency binary search font fitting algorithm with SHA-256 digests 14297c41959cf0ac87725c0936585d4601183a1cab42bc8e964aa355ee2f1b19 and 20864a8bb30292dca25d4a228fe4fc0de5954406d15f5ef1ef4c84f0e95168e2.
